div.p: The science of household management differs from that of politics not only as much as a household differs from a city (for these are their respective subject-matters), but also in that politics involves many rulers, whereas household management is a monarchy.

Now some arts are divided, so that it does not belong to the same art to make an instrument and to use what has been made, as with a lyre and flutes; but it belongs to politics both to establish a city from the beginning and to make good use of one already existing. It is clear, then, that it likewise belongs to household management both to acquire a household and to make use of it.

A city, then, is a collection of households, land, and property sufficient in itself for living well. This is evident; for whenever men are unable to attain this, the community too is dissolved. Moreover, it is for the sake of this that they come together; and that for the sake of which each thing exists and has come into being is in fact its essence.
It is clear, therefore, that household management is prior in origin to politics, as is its function; for a household is a part of a city.
We must consider, then, household management and what its function is.

The component parts of a household are human beings and property. Since the nature of each thing is first observed in its smallest elements, the same will hold true of a household. Thus, according to Hesiod, there must first be
First of all a house, and a wife, and an ox for the plow. Hes. WD 405 For the latter is the first requirement for sustenance, and the former for free persons. Consequently, one must manage well the relations concerning one's wife; and this consists in making her the sort of person she ought to be.

Of property, the first care is that which accords with nature. According to nature, agriculture comes first, and second come all occupations derived from the earth, such as mining and any other of the kind. Agriculture is foremost because it is just; for it does not gain wealth from men, either willingly, as in retail trade and wage-earning occupations, or unwillingly, as in war. Furthermore, it is also natural; for by nature sustenance comes to all from their mother, and so to men from the earth.

In addition, it contributes greatly to courage; for unlike the mechanical crafts, it does not render bodies useless, but rather capable of living in the open air and enduring toil, and moreover capable of facing danger against enemies; for farmers alone have their possessions outside the fortifications.

Of the cares concerning human beings, the first is that concerning a wife; for the partnership of female and male is above all natural. We have laid down elsewhere that nature aims at producing many such creatures, just as with each species of animals; and it is impossible for the female without the male, or the male without the female, to accomplish this; so that their partnership has come together out of necessity.

In the other animals this exists without reason, only to the extent that they share in nature, and solely for the sake of begetting offspring; but in the tamer and more intelligent animals it is more clearly articulated (for mutual help, goodwill, and cooperation are seen more clearly among them),

and in man most of all, because female and male cooperate with one another not merely for existence, but also for living well. And the having of children is not merely a service rendered to nature, but also brings advantage; for the labor that parents spend while they are able upon their helpless children, they receive back again in old age from their able children when they themselves are helpless.

At the same time, nature also fulfills eternal existence through this cycle, since she cannot do so in individual number, but only in species. Thus the nature of each—both the man and the woman—has been prearranged by the divine for partnership. For they are distinguished by not having powers useful for all the same tasks, but in some respects for opposite ones, yet tending toward the same end: the divine made the one stronger and the other weaker, so that the one might be more watchful through fear and the other more ready to defend through courage, and that the one might procure what comes from outside while the other preserves what is within; and for work, the one is capable of sedentary labor yet weak for outdoor endurance, while the other is less suited for quiet life yet healthy in active movement; and regarding children, their begetting is shared, while their benefit is distinct—for to the one belongs their nurture, and to the other their education.

First, then, come the rules toward a wife, and not to wrong her; for in this way a man will not be wronged himself either. This is what the common law also prescribes, as the Pythagoreans say: that one ought least of all to seem to wrong a wife, as she is a suppliant and led from the hearth. Wrongdoing on a husband's part consists in liaisons outside the home.

As for marital intercourse, it should neither be such that she feels no need nor such that she cannot remain calm in his absence, but he should accustom her so that she is content whether he is present or absent. Well spoken too is the saying of Hesiod:
Marry a maiden, that you may teach her discreet ways. Hes. WD 699 For dissimilarities of character are least conducive to affection.

Regarding adornment, just as they ought not to approach one another with ostentation in character, so neither should they in body; for intercourse accompanied by artificial adornment is no different from that of tragic actors in their stage costumes.

Of possessions, the first and most necessary is that which is best and most fitted for household management; and this is the human being. Therefore one must first acquire good slaves. There are two kinds of slaves: the overseer and the laborer. Since we observe that education shapes the character of the young, it is necessary also to procure and train those to whom the more liberal tasks are to be assigned.

One's dealings with slaves should be such as neither to allow them to grow insolent nor to treat them harshly; to the more liberal sort one should grant a share of honor, and to the laborers an abundance of food. And since drinking wine makes even free men insolent, and many nations abstain from it even for free men—as do the Carthaginians on campaign—it is clear that of wine one should give them either none at all or very rarely.

There being three things—work, punishment, and food—to have food without punishment or work breeds insolence; while to have work and punishment without food is oppressive and produces weakness. It remains, then, to provide work and sufficient food; for it is impossible to rule men without wages, and a slave's wages are his food.
Just as with others, when the better receive no better treatment and there are no prizes for virtue and penalties for vice, they become worse, so it is also with household slaves.

Accordingly, one must keep watch and distribute or withhold everything according to merit—food, clothing, leisure, and punishments—imitating in word and deed the practice of physicians in prescribing medicine, while bearing in mind that food is not medicine because it is taken continuously.
The best nationalities for work would be those neither too cowardly nor too spirited; for both are harmful, since the overly cowardly lack endurance and the high-spirited are not easily governed.

It is also right that a definite goal be set for all; for it is both just and advantageous that freedom be offered as a prize, since they are willing to work hard when there is a prize and a fixed time. One should also take hostages from them by allowing them to have children, and not acquire many of the same nationality, just as in cities; and sacrifices and holidays should be held more for the sake of the slaves than of the free, for slaves have a greater share in that for the sake of which such things were instituted.

There are four qualities that a household manager must possess with respect to wealth. He must be able both to acquire and to preserve; otherwise there is no use in acquiring, for that is drawing water with a sieve and the proverbial leaky jar. Further, he must be able to arrange his possessions in order and to make use of them, since it is for the sake of these latter ends that we need the former.

Each of these kinds of property should be kept distinct, and productive possessions should exceed unproductive ones, and enterprises should be distributed so as not to risk everything at once. For preservation, it is advantageous to follow both the Persian and the Laconian methods. The Attic system of household management is also useful: they sell their produce and buy what they need, and there is no storehouse in smaller households.

The Persian system was to have everything ordered and to inspect everything oneself, in accordance with what Dion used to say about Dionysius; for no one cares for another's property as he does for his own, so that as far as possible one should attend to supervision in person. Both the Persian's and the Libyan's sayings are apt: the former, when asked what best fattens a horse, replied, The master's eye; and the Libyan, when asked what kind of manure is best, replied, The master's footprints.

Some matters, then, the husband himself should inspect, and others the wife, according to the division of household duties between them. In small households this need be done only occasionally, but in those managed by overseers it must be done frequently; for without a good example there can be no good imitation, whether in other matters or in stewardship, since it is impossible for overseers to be diligent when their masters are not diligent.

Since these habits are both noble for virtue and useful for household management, masters ought to rise earlier than their servants and go to sleep later; a house, like a city, should never be left unguarded; whatever needs to be done should be neglected neither by night nor by day; and rising before dawn is beneficial for health, household management, and philosophy.

On small estates, then, the Attic method of disposing of the produce is useful; on large estates, once what is expended annually and what is expended monthly have been separated—and similarly regarding the use of utensils needed daily and those needed rarely—these should be handed over to the overseers. In addition, an inspection of them should be held at intervals, so that what is intact and what is missing may not escape notice.

A house should be constructed with a view to one's possessions, and to the health and well-being of its occupants: by possessions I mean what kind of quarters suit produce and clothing, and of produce what suits dry stores and what suits liquid stores, and of other possessions what suits living things and what suits inanimate things, slaves and free, women and men, strangers and citizens. And for well-being and health, it should be airy in summer and sunny in winter.

Such a house would face south, sheltered from the north, and not be of equal depth and breadth. In large households it also seems useful to have a doorkeeper who is unfit for other work, to keep safe what is brought in and taken out. For convenience in using utensils, the Laconian method is best: each single thing should lie in its own place, so that being ready to hand it need not be searched for.

Whoever intends to manage any economy properly must not be unacquainted with the regions in which he operates, must be naturally gifted, and by deliberate choice must be industrious and just; for if any of these qualities is lacking, he will make many mistakes in the business he handles.
There are four types of economy, to classify them in outline (for we shall find that all others fall under these): royal, satrapic, civic, and private.

Of these, the largest and simplest is the royal, , the most varied and easiest is the civic, and the smallest and most varied is the private. Necessarily they have many things in common with one another, but we must examine the features that are most distinctive to each.
First, then, let us look at the royal economy. This has universal authority, and comprises four departments: coinage, exports, imports, and expenditures.

Under each of these indeed, concerning coinage, I mean what kind should be issued and when its value should be raised or lowered; concerning exports and imports, when and what commodities received from the satraps in tribute it will be profitable for the king to dispose of; and concerning expenditures, which should be curtailed and when, and whether expenses should be paid in coin or in goods purchasable with coin.
Second is the satrapic economy. Of this there are six kinds of revenue: from land, from the special products of the country, from trading centers, from taxes, from cattle, and from other sources.

Of these themselves, the first and best is that from the land (this is what some call land-rent and others the tithe); the second is that from special local products—in one place gold, in another silver, in another copper, in another whatever can be produced; the third is that from trading centers; the fourth is that arising from overland tolls and market dues; the fifth is that from cattle, called the yield-tax and tithe; and the sixth is that from other sources, called the poll-tax and artisan-tax.
Third is the civic economy. Of this the best revenue is that from the special products of the country, next that from trading centers and transit dues, and next that from ordinary recurring taxes.

Fourth and last is the private economy. This is irregular because it cannot be managed toward a single aim, and smallest because both its revenues and its expenditures are slight. Of this economy itself, the best revenue is that from land, the second that from other investments, and the third that from money at interest. Apart from these, there is one rule common to all economies which deserves no casual attention, and especially in this one: that expenditures must not exceed revenues.

Now that we have stated the divisions, we must next consider whether the satrapy or city with which we are dealing is able to bear all the revenues we have just distinguished or the greatest of them, and make use of these; and after that, which revenues do not exist at all yet could be created, or being small at present could be made larger, or of the expenditures currently being made, which and how many could be cut without harming the whole.

We have now spoken of the types of economy and their parts; and we have also collected whatever measures men of former times have taken to raise money or have skillfully administered, insofar as we considered them noteworthy. For we do not think this record useless either, since sometimes one of these examples will apply to the affairs a man is managing himself.

Cypselus of Corinth, having vowed to Zeus that if he became master of the city he would dedicate to him all the property of the Corinthians, ordered them to register their estates. When they had registered them, he took a tenth part from each and bade them work with the remainder. When a year had gone by, he did the very same thing again, so that in ten years he possessed everything he had consecrated, while the Corinthians had acquired fresh wealth.

Lygdamis of Naxos, after banishing exiles, since no one would buy their properties except at a low price, sold them back to the exiles themselves. And the votive offerings belonging to them that lay half-finished in various workshops he sold to the exiles and to anyone else who wished, with the right to have the buyer's name inscribed on them.

The Byzantines, being in need of money, sold the public sacred precincts—the fertile ones for a term of years, and the barren ones in perpetuity; and similarly the lands of religious guilds and clans, and all that lay within private estates, for the owners of the surrounding land bought them at a high price. To the guilds they gave other public lands around the gymnasium, the marketplace, or the harbor, as well as the market stalls where anyone sold goods, the sea-fisheries, and the state salt-monopoly, and the professions of jugglers, diviners, drug-sellers, and other such people ; and they ordained that these should pay a third part of their earnings. They also sold the exchange of currency to a single bank, and no one else was permitted either to sell to another or to buy from another, on pain of confiscation.

Having a law that no one could be a citizen unless born of citizen parents on both sides, when they needed money they decreed that anyone born of one citizen parent might become a citizen upon paying thirty minas.

When they fell into a grain shortage and lacked money, they detained the ships sailing from the Pontus; after some time, when the merchants grew indignant, they paid them interest at ten percent, and required buyers to pay an extra ten percent above the price.

When certain resident aliens had lent money on the security of real estate, although they did not have the right to own land, they decreed that anyone who wished might acquire full ownership of the property by paying a third of the loan to the state.

Hippias the Athenian put up for sale upper stories that projected over the public streets, as well as steps, railings, and doors that opened outward; the owners of the properties bought them, and in this way a large sum of money was collected.
He also declared the existing Athenian coinage invalid, and fixing a rate of exchange ordered it to be brought to him; when they met to strike a new die, he reissued the very same silver.

And for all who were about to spend money on a trierarchy, a phylarchy, a choregia, or any other such public liturgy, he fixed a moderate assessment and allowed anyone who wished to pay this and be enrolled among those who had performed the liturgy.

He also ordained that for every person who died, a choenix of barley, another of wheat, and an obol should be brought to the priestess of Athena on the Acropolis, and the same whenever a child was born.

The Athenians living in Potidaea, needing money for the war, ordered everyone to register his property—not all together in his own deme, but each piece of property in the district where it lay, so that the poor could assess themselves at a lower rate; and whoever had no property at all was to assess his person at two minas. On this basis each paid the full tax assessed upon him to the city.

Sosipolis of Antissa moreover, when the city needed money and since they were accustomed to celebrate the Dionysia with great splendor—spending much on it with preparations throughout the year, including costly sacrificial victims—persuaded them, as the festival was close at hand, to vow to Dionysus that they would offer double the next year, and to gather together and sell the present victims. Thus a considerable sum of money was raised for their need.

The people of Lampsacus, when a large fleet of triremes was expected to arrive, while a medimnus of barley-meal stood at four drachmas, ordered the retail dealers to sell it at six drachmas, and a chous of olive oil, which stood at three drachmas, at four drachmas and three obols, and wine and other commodities in like manner. The private dealer received the old price, and the city took the surplus, thus gaining plenty of money.

The Heracleots, when sending forty ships against the tyrants of the Bosporus and being short of money, bought up from the merchants all the grain, olive oil, wine, and other provisions on credit, fixing a date by which they would pay the price. The merchants were well pleased not to retail their goods piecemeal but to sell their entire cargoes in bulk; and the Heracleots, giving no pay in advance, brought along but the provisions in merchant vessels, and appointed a paymaster on each of the ships. When they reached enemy territory, the soldiers bought everything from these paymasters. Thus in fact the silver was collected back before the generals issued pay again, so that the very same sum of silver was paid out over and over until they returned home.

The Lacedaemonians, when the Samians begged them for money to aid their return from exile, decreed that they themselves, their servants, and their pack animals should fast for one day, and that each should give to the Samians the amount he ordinarily spent.

The Chalcedonians, having many mercenaries in their city to whom they owed pay that they could not discharge, proclaimed that if any citizen or resident alien had a right of reprisal against any city or individual and wished to enforce it, he should register it. Many having registered, they seized ships sailing into the Pontus on a plausible pretext, fixing a date at which they said they would render an account of them. When a large sum of money had been collected, they paid off the soldiers and held trials concerning the reprisals, and to those who had been unjustly despoiled the city made restitution from its revenues.

The Cyzicenes, during a civil war in which the democratic party prevailed and the wealthy were arrested, owing money to their soldiers, decreed not to put the prisoners to death, but to exact money from them and send them into exile.

The Chians, who had a law requiring all debts to be registered in the public records, being in need of money decreed that debtors should repay their loans to the city, and that the city should pay the interest to the creditors out of its revenues until it was able to repay the principal as well.

Mausolus, tyrant of Caria, when the Great King sent to him demanding tribute, called together the wealthiest men in the country and told them that the King was demanding the tribute, while he himself lacked funds. Men whom he had suborned immediately pledged how much each would contribute; and when they had done this, the wealthier men, partly out of shame and partly out of fear, pledged and contributed much more than these.

Needing money again, he called an assembly of the Mylasians and told them that his mother-city here was unwalled, while the King was marching against him. He therefore ordered the Mylasians to bring each as much money as possible, claiming that by what they contributed now they would save the rest as well. When a large sum had been brought in, he kept the money, and declared that the god did not permit him to build the wall for the present.

Condalus, the lieutenant of Mausolus, whenever anyone offered him a sheep, pig, or calf as he passed through the country, wrote down the giver's name and the date and told him to take it back home and rear it until he returned; then, when he thought enough time had passed, he demanded back both the reared animal and its calculated produce. He also sold the produce of trees that overhung or fell onto the royal roads.

Whenever one of the soldiers died, he exacted a gate-toll of one drachma for the body; thus he both obtained money from this source and prevented the officers from deceiving him as to when a soldier had died.

Observing that the Lycians were fond of wearing long hair, he announced that a letter had arrived from the King ordering him to send hair for wigs, and that he had been instructed by Mausolus to shear them. He said, however, that if they were willing to pay him a fixed poll-tax, he would send for hair from Greece; they gladly paid what he asked, and a great sum of money was collected from a large populace.

Aristotle of Rhodes, governor of Phocaea, being short of money and seeing that there were two factions among the Phocaeans, held secret talks with one faction, claiming that the other faction was offering him money to tilt affairs in their favor, but that he preferred to take it from these and hand over the administration of the city to them. Hearing this, those present immediately raised the money he demanded and gave it to him. He then showed the other faction what he had received from the first, and they declared they would give no less. Having taken money from both sides, he reconciled them with one another.

Seeing also that the citizens had many lawsuits and grave grievances of long standing because of war, he set up a court and proclaimed that whoever did not bring his suit within a time limit he fixed would no longer have any trial for past claims. Then, by securing for himself the court deposits of many suits and appeals with penalties, and taking money from both sides through intermediaries, he gathered no small sum of money.

The Clazomenians, suffering from a grain shortage and lacking money, decreed that private citizens who possessed olive oil should lend it to the city at interest; for this crop is abundant in their territory. When they lent it, the city hired ships and sent them to the trading ports, whence grain came back to them, the value of the oil serving as security.

Owing twenty talents in pay to their mercenaries and being unable to pay, they were paying the officers four talents a year in interest; when they saw they were reducing none of the principal while continually spending to no purpose, they minted iron coinage to the silver value of twenty talents, and distributing it proportionally to the wealthiest citizens in the city, they received an equal amount of silver from them. Thus private citizens had currency to spend on daily needs, and the city was freed from its debt. Next, out of its revenues, the city paid them interest and continually redeemed a portion for each in turn, taking back the iron coins.

The Selymbrians, needing money when they had a law forbidding the export of grain during a famine, and having a stock of old grain, decreed that private citizens should hand over their grain to the city at the fixed price, each keeping a year's supply for himself; then they granted permission to export to anyone who wished, fixing a price that seemed advantageous to them.

The Abydenes, when their land lay uncultivated owing to civil strife and the resident aliens would advance them nothing because they were still in debt, decreed that anyone who wished might lend money to the farmers to work the land, on the terms that these lenders should have first claim to repayment from the harvest, while the earlier creditors should be paid from what remained.
The Ephesians, needing money, enacted a law that women should not wear gold, and should lend to the city whatever gold they then possessed.
They also fixed a sum of money to be paid for certain columns in the temple, and allowed the name of the man who paid the silver to be inscribed as the dedicator.

Dionysius of Syracuse, wishing to raise money, called an assembly and declared that he had seen Demeter, who commanded that the women's jewelry be brought to her temple. He himself, he said, had already done this with the jewelry of the women of his own household, and he urged the others to do likewise, lest some wrath come from the goddess; anyone who failed to do so, he declared, would be guilty of sacrilege. When everyone had brought up what they had, out of fear of both the goddess and Dionysius, he sacrificed to the goddess and carried off the jewelry as a loan from her. After some time, when the women began wearing gold again, he ordered any woman who wished to wear gold to dedicate a fixed sum in the temple.

When about to build triremes, he knew he would need money. Calling an assembly, he said that a certain city was being betrayed to him, for which he needed funds, and he asked the citizens to contribute two staters each; they contributed. After an interval of two or three days, pretending that the enterprise had failed, he praised them and gave back to each what he had contributed. By doing this he won the citizens' confidence. Then again expecting to get it back, they contributed; and he took it and kept it for his shipbuilding.

Being short of silver, he struck a coinage of tin, and calling an assembly spoke at length in favor of the new coinage; they voted, even against their will, that each would accept what he took as silver rather than tin.

Needing money again, he asked the citizens to contribute to him; they said they had none. He therefore brought out his own household furnishings and put them up for sale, as if doing so out of poverty; as the Syracusans bought them, he recorded what each man bought, and once they had paid the price, he ordered each to bring back the article he had bought.

When the citizens stopped raising cattle because of the taxes, he declared that he had enough revenue for the time being, and that those who now acquired cattle would be exempt from tax. When many quickly acquired large herds in the expectation of holding them tax-free, as soon as he judged the time ripe he ordered an assessment and imposed a tax. Indignant at having been deceived, the citizens began slaughtering and selling them. When he countered this by limiting the number that might be slaughtered each day, they turned to offering them as sacrifices; whereupon he forbade the sacrificing of any female animal.
Needing money again, he ordered all estates of orphans to be registered in property with him; and when others had registered them, he used their funds until each orphan came of age.

After capturing Rhegium, he called an assembly and declared that they would justly be enslaved by him, yet now he would release them if he recovered his war expenses plus three minas per person. The Rhegians brought out into the open everything they had hidden, and the poor borrowed from the wealthier and from foreigners to raise the money he demanded. Once he had taken this from them, he nonetheless sold all the people into slavery and seized all the valuables that had previously been hidden and were now brought to light.

Having borrowed money from the citizens on a promise of repayment, when they demanded it back he ordered everyone to bring whatever silver he possessed to him, fixing death as the penalty for failure. When the silver was brought in, he restamped it and issued the drachma at the value of two drachmas, and thus paid off both the previous debt they had brought in to him.

Sailing to Etruria with a hundred ships, he took from the temple of Leucothea much gold and silver and no small amount of other treasure. Knowing that the sailors also had much plunder, he made a proclamation that each should bring half of what he had to him and might keep the other half, fixing death as the penalty for failure to comply. Supposing that by handing in half they would keep the remainder, the sailors brought it in without fear; but as soon as he had taken that, he ordered them to bring in the other half as well.

The Mendaeans used the revenues accruing from their harbors and other dues for the administration of the city, while they did not collect the taxes on land and houses, but merely registered the owners; whenever they needed money, the debtors paid up, having thus profited in the meantime by the interest-free use of the money.

When they were also at war with the Olynthians and needed money, as they possessed slaves, they decreed that each citizen should keep one female and one male slave and sell the rest to the city, so that private citizens might thus lend money to the state.

Callistratus in Macedonia, when the harbor dues were generally farmed out for twenty talents, caused them to fetch double that sum; for observing that only the wealthier men ever bought them because they had to provide sureties worth a talent each for the twenty talents, he proclaimed that anyone who wished might bid and provide sureties for a third part, or for whatever amount each could persuade the authorities to accept.

Timotheus of Athens, while fighting against the Olynthians and lacking silver, minted bronze coins and distributed them to his soldiers. When the soldiers grew indignant, he told them that the merchants and market-dealers would sell them everything on the same terms as before; and to the merchants he announced that with whatever bronze coin they received they might buy both the produce of the country and the goods brought in from plunder, and whatever bronze coin remained on their hands they could bring back to him and receive silver.

While campaigning around Corcyra and in financial straits, when his soldiers demanded their pay, refused to obey him, and threatened to go over to the enemy, he called an assembly and declared that silver could not reach him because of the winter storms, whereas he actually had such abundant resources that he was making them a free gift of the three months' rations already advanced to them. Supposing that Timotheus would never give away so much money unless funds were truly on their way to him, they kept quiet about their pay until he had accomplished what he wished.

While besieging Samos, he sold the crops and produce of the fields to the Samians themselves, and thus obtained ample money to pay his soldiers. And when provisions grew scarce in the camp because of new arrivals, he forbade the sale of milled grain or of any measure less than a medimnus, or of any liquid less than a metretes. Consequently, the taxiarchs and lochagi bought in bulk and distributed to the soldiers, while newcomers brought their own provisions with them and sold whatever they had left over when they departed; and thus the soldiers were well supplied with provisions.

Didales the Persian, having soldiers under him, was able to supply their daily needs from enemy territory, but having no coin to pay them, when they demanded it after their pay had fallen into arrears, he devised the following stratagem. Calling an assembly, he declared that he was not short of money, but had a supply in a certain place, naming it. Breaking camp, he marched toward it; then, when he drew near the place, he went ahead into it and took from the temples there all the embossed silver plate they contained. Loading the mules so that they appeared to be carrying silver, with these vessels peeking out, he marched on. Seeing this and supposing that the entire load was silver, the soldiers took heart in the expectation of receiving their pay. He then said they must go to Amisus to have it coined; and the road to Amisus was a march of many days in winter. During all this time he made use of the army while giving them only their rations.
He also kept in his own employ the craftsmen in the camp and the peddlers who traded in anything; no one else was allowed to do any of these things.

Chabrias of Athens advised Tachos, king of Egypt, when he was setting out on campaign and needed money, to tell the priests that some of the temples and the majority of the priests would have to be abolished because of the expense. Hearing this, and each wishing his own temple to remain intact, the priests offered him money even from their private funds. When he had received money from all of them, Chabrias advised him to order them to spend a tenth of what they had formerly spent on the temple and themselves, and to lend the rest to him until the war against the Great King was settled.

He also advised him to order everyone to pay a fixed contribution on each house, and likewise a poll-tax on each person; on the sale of grain, both seller and buyer were to pay an obol per artaba above the price; and from ships, workshops, and all who carried on any other trade, he ordered a tenth part of their earnings to be paid.

When he was about to march out of the country, he advised him to order anyone who possessed uncoined silver or gold to bring it to him; when most had brought it in, he told the king to use this money and to refer the lenders to the nomarchs, so that they might be repaid out of the taxes.

Iphicrates of Athens, when Cotys had assembled an army, procured money for him in the following way. He advised him to order each of the men under his rule to sow for him a plot of land requiring three medimni of seed. When this was done, a great quantity of grain was harvested; bringing it down to the trading ports, he sold it and obtained plenty of money.

Cotys of Thrace sought to borrow money from the Perinthians to raise troops, but the Perinthians would not give it to him. He therefore asked them at least to provide citizens as garrisons for certain fortresses, so that he might use the soldiers currently garrisoning them. They readily did this, thinking they would become masters of the fortresses. Cotys, however, threw the men they sent into prison and told the Perinthians to send the money he had asked to borrow from them if they wished to recover their citizens.

Mentor of Rhodes, having captured Hermias and seized his territories, left the stewards appointed by Hermias in their posts. When they had all regained confidence and had brought out with them whatever they had previously hidden or deposited elsewhere, he arrested them and stripped them of everything they had.

Memnon of Rhodes, having gained control of Lampsacus and needing money, assessed a sum of silver upon the richest citizens, telling them they would be reimbursed by the rest of the citizens; when the other citizens had paid their contributions, he ordered them to lend this sum to him as well, fixing a date by which he would repay them.

Needing money again, he asked them to contribute, promising repayment out of the public revenues; they contributed, expecting a quick return. When the installments of the revenues came in, he said that he needed these too, and would repay them later with interest.

From the soldiers serving under him he deducted six days' rations and pay per year, claiming that on those days they did no guard duty, no marching, and incurred no expense—referring to the omitted days of the calendar.

And whereas previously he had issued rations to the soldiers on the second day of the month, in the first month he passed over three days, in the next five, and continued advancing the date in this way until he reached the thirtieth.

Charidemus of Oreus, holding certain towns in Aeolis when Artabazus marched against him, needed money for his soldiers. At first the inhabitants contributed to him, but then declared they had no more. Charidemus ordered the town he thought wealthiest also to send away any coin or other valuable property they possessed to another town, promising to provide an escort; and at the same time he was seen openly doing the same himself. Persuaded by this, the people set out; leading them a short distance from the city, he searched what they had, took what he needed, and led them back to the town.

He also issued a proclamation in the cities he ruled that no one should keep any weapon in his house, on pain of paying a fine he announced, yet paid no heed and took no action. Thinking that he had issued the proclamation to no purpose, the people kept whatever weapons they happened to own in their houses. Suddenly he conducted a search of the houses and exacted the fine from everyone in whose house he found a weapon.

A certain Philoxenus of Macedonia, satrap of Caria, needing money, announced that he intended to celebrate the Dionysia, designated the wealthiest Carians as choregi, and instructed them what they must prepare. Seeing them dismayed, he secretly sent agents to ask what they were willing to pay to be relieved of the liturgy. They offered to pay much more than they expected it would cost, in order not to be troubled and kept away from their private affairs. Taking from them what they offered, he enrolled others in their place, until he had obtained from them what he wanted, with a surplus from each group.

Evaeses the Syrian, satrap of Egypt, learning that the nomarchs were about to revolt from him, summoned them to the palace and hanged them all, while ordering their relatives to be told that they were in prison. Each of the relatives accordingly negotiated for his own kinsman and ransomed the prisoners for money; having struck a bargain for each and received the agreed sum, he returned the corpse to each family.

Cleomenes of Alexandria, satrap of Egypt, when a severe famine broke out in other lands while Egypt was only moderately affected, banned the export of grain. When the nomarchs declared they would be unable to pay their taxes if grain were not exported, he permitted export but imposed a heavy duty on grain, so that if not he collected a large tax on a small export, while the nomarchs were deprived of their excuse.

While he was sailing through the nome in which the crocodile is worshipped as a god, one of his slaves was snatched by a crocodile. Summoning the priests, he said that since he had been wronged first he would take vengeance on the crocodiles, and ordered them to be hunted. The priests, so that their god might not be treated with contempt, gathered as much gold as they could and gave it to him, and thus he desisted.

When King Alexander instructed him to found a city near Pharos and to transfer thither the trading center that had previously been at Canobus, he sailed down to Canobus and told the priests and property owners there that he had come for the purpose of relocating them. Now the priests and residents raised money and gave it to him so that he would leave their trading center where it was. Taking the money, he departed for the time being; later, when his preparations for building were ready, he sailed down again and demanded an exorbitant sum of money, saying that this was the difference to him between having the trading center at his new city and leaving it there. When they said they could not pay it, he relocated them.

Having sent someone to make a purchase and learning that the man had bought cheaply but intended to charge him inflated prices, he told the buyer's associates that he had heard the man had bought the goods at excessive prices and that he would therefore pay no attention to him, at the same time railing at his stupidity with feigned anger. Hearing this, they told him he ought not to believe what people said against the man until he arrived and rendered his account. When the buyer arrived, they reported to him what Cleomenes had said; wishing to prove himself both to them and to Cleomenes, he turned in the exact prices at which he had actually bought the goods.

When grain was selling in the country at ten drachmas, he summoned the producers and asked at what price they were willing to work for him; they said for less than what they sold to the merchants. He ordered them to deliver it to him at the same price they sold to others, while he himself fixed the price of grain at thirty-two drachmas and sold it at that rate.

He also summoned the priests and declared that the irregular expenditure on temples in the country was excessive, so that some of the temples and the majority of the priests would have to be abolished. The priests, both individually and collectively, gave him the sacred funds, believing that he truly intended to do this and each wishing his own temple to remain standing and himself to remain a priest.

Antimenes of Rhodes, being appointed by Alexander in charge of the roads around Babylon, raised money as follows. There being an ancient law in Babylonia imposing a tithe on imports, though no one enforced it, he watched for the arrival of all the satraps and soldiers who were expected, as well as many envoys, invited craftsmen, others bringing goods or traveling on private business, and many gifts being brought up, and exacted the tithe in accordance with the existing law.

Again, to raise money from the slaves in the camp, he invited anyone who wished to register his slave at whatever value he chose, paying eight drachmas a year, with the guarantee that if the slave ran away, the owner would receive the value at which he had registered him. Many slaves were registered, bringing in no small sum of silver; and if any slave ran away, he ordered the satrap of the in which the camp lay to recover him or pay his value to the owner.

Ophelas of Olynthus, having appointed a superintendent for the Athribite nome, was approached by the nomarchs of that district, who said they were willing to pay much more themselves and asked him to dismiss the superintendent currently in office. Asking them whether they would be able to pay what they promised, and receiving their assurance, he left the superintendent in office and ordered him to collect the taxes at the higher rate they themselves had assessed. Thus he neither appeared to dishonor the man he had appointed nor to impose heavier taxes on them than they themselves had fixed, while he himself received many times more money.

Pythocles of Athens advised the Athenians that the city should take over the lead from the mines of Laurium from private producers at two drachmas, the price at which they were selling it, and then fix the price at six drachmas and sell it themselves.

Chabrias, when crews had been enrolled for one hundred and twenty ships, though Tachos needed only sixty, ordered the men from the sixty ships remaining behind to provide two months' rations for those who sailed, or else to sail themselves. Wishing to stay at home, they paid what he ordered.

Antimenes ordered the satraps to replenish the storehouses along the royal roads according to the law of the land; and whenever an army or other body of men passed through without the King, he sent an agent of his own to sell the supplies from the storehouses.

Cleomenes, as the first of the month approached when he was due to issue rations to the soldiers, purposely sailed away; then, when the month was well advanced, he sailed back and distributed the rations, and in the following month skipped payment until the first of the month after that. Because the soldiers had just recently received their rations, they kept quiet, while by shifting one month per year he continually cheated them of a month's pay.

Stabelbius, the of the Mysians, owing pay to his soldiers, called together and said that he had no need of the rank and file, but only of the officers; and whenever he needed soldiers, he would give each officer money and send him out to recruit mercenaries, and he would rather pay to the officers the wages that had to be given to the men. He therefore ordered each of them to send his own contingent out of the country. Supposing that this would be a source of profit for themselves, the officers sent the soldiers away as he had ordered. After a short interval, he called the officers together and told them that just as a flute-player is of no use without a chorus, neither are officers without rank and file; and he ordered them to leave the country.

Dionysius, making the rounds of the temples, whenever he saw a gold or silver table set out, would order a libation to be poured to the Good Spirit and then order the table to be carried off; and whenever statues held out a libation bowl, he would say "I accept" and order it to be taken away. He also stripped the golden cloaks and the wreaths from the statues, claiming that he was giving them lighter and more fragrant ones; and he then put white cloaks and wreaths of white violets upon them.
